segments.speaker: Paula Kami · MC, MINISPORTS

segments.text: So on top of standing on business, I believe in Africa, we're also standing on talent. We're standing on ambition. We're standing on hard work and the dare to be different.

segments.text: The dare to be different and, you know, do things more our way. And that is exactly what today's conversation is about. Africa has incredibly grown in sporting talent.

segments.speaker: Paula Kami · MC, MINISPORTS
segments.text: We have athletes representing from different countries and going on the international stage. Young people with extraordinary potential and sporting communities that continue to inspire and bring people together. Today is about bringing generations together, learning from experience, challenging existing ideas, and importantly, identifying particular commitments.

segments.speaker: Paula Kami · MC, MINISPORTS
segments.text: To set the context for our discussion, we are honored to have with us a leader who brings an important continental perspective on the future of our sport. It is therefore my pleasure to invite Her Excellency, the Honorable, if I may, to open us up with this keynote speech. The Minister of Seminar.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Good morning. Good morning. Excellency, Minister of Youth and Lands of the Republic of Rwanda.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Excellency, Minister of Sports of the Republic of Rwanda. Excellencies, Ambassadors, Ministers, dear partners, entrepreneurs, ladies and gentlemen, leaders of sports and institutions. Dear young people, it's my pleasure to open this session.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: It speaks to the threat of our continent's future. How one generation's legacy can serve the next to build a sports economy. The future of the sports economy.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: First of all, I would like to thank the government of the Republic of Rwanda for this initiative and their hospitality. Congratulations to the whole team that prepared this so inspiring program. By bringing us together around the scene, the organizers invite us to look at sports differently and to watch the role it can play in Africa's economic transformation.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Sport is not merely a space for competition, leisure or performance. It is also an industry, a growing market and a source of jobs for our youth. Ladies and gentlemen, Africa is the youngest continent in the world.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: More than 60% of its population is under 25. Its usefulness, the popular passion for sports and our globally recognized talents in this area are considerable assets. Yet these assets remain underutilized.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: The global sports economy is worth roughly 2.3 trillion dollars per year. Whereas in Africa, sports teams account for only about 0.5% of the country's GDP. Most sporting goods used in Africa are manufactured elsewhere.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: However, every match and every competition sustains numerous progressions. Equipment, manufacturing, digital ticketing, broadcasting, tourism, hospitality, sports medicine, data analytics and facility management. The report recently published by Agence Francaise de Développement, the International Olympic Committee and the World Bank confirm this.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: The sports economy will grow in Africa if we succeed in fostering a network for global youth. Our challenge, therefore, is to turn young African professionals into structured activities, viable businesses and decent jobs. This is urgent.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Nearly one in four young Africans aged 15 to 24 is currently not in employment, education or training. Ladies and gentlemen, across the continent, several countries have already embarked on this transformation. Right here in Rwanda, our host country, the sports tourism strategy and the hosting of major events such as the Basketball Africa finals at BK Arena in Kigali have given rise to a service economy in Rwanda.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: The title won last May in Kigali by Rwanda Club RSSB Tigers is a prime illustration of this. That also is true when hosting the SARA Conference. In Côte d'Ivoire, hosting AACOM, Accelerated Infrastructure Modernization, it is accompanied by the AGORA program which aims to improve neighbourhoods with local sports and cultural spaces that generate economic activity.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: In Morocco, sport has become a driver of territorial and industrial development, combining high-level training sectors, the hosting of global competitions and the structuring of peaceful life and well-being. These are tangible examples. But let's go further.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Senegal runs to a historic challenge. From October 31st to November 30th, they hosted the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event ever staged on Africa's soil. For two weeks, three of Senegal's cities welcomed the world's brightest young athletes.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Many viewed this event as impossible. We delivered on it. And we showed that Africa can organize the top-level international competition using its own expertise and its own businesses.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Of course! That AACOM leaves us with three lessons. First, major sporting events must be markets for our local businesses. In total, 121 Senegalese companies won contracts from the organizing committee in logistics, construction, communications, and technology.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: They secured 18.2 billion EXOF, or nearly two-thirds of the total funds initially committed for the organization. An international competition can therefore strengthen Africa's SMEs. We must now help them export this know-how to other markets across the continent.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Second, investing in sports means investing in youth skills and employment. 6,000 volunteers were brought on board of this project. More than 400 young Senegalese and African professionals were trained by the DACA 2026 Learning Academy and gained hands-on experience.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: They now form a talent pool for event management, for marketing, audiovisual production, and sports venue operations. Third, sports infrastructure must remain after the event. Renovated or newly built facilities must not become a burden on our public finances.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: The Olympic Village built on the campus of the university was designed to return to its university purpose after the Games. Renovated venues for the event must remain open to young people, schools, and clubs. Ladies and gentlemen, to bring an African sports industry into being, we know our five priorities to my view.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Facilitate young entrepreneurs' access to financing through seed funds and incubators dedicated to sport techniques, startup equipment makers and organizers. Develop African value chains. Professionalize sports careers.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Make sports tourism a rigorous representation of local development. Measure the economic contribution of sports through satellites and dams. Through satellites and dams.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Dear young people, the African sports economy will be built in stadiums, but also in our training centers, workshops, digital incubators, and neighborhood facilities. To achieve this, we need strong partnerships among governments, the private sector, financial institutions, federations, universities, but also youth organizations. The legacy of DACA 2026 will be measured, of course, by medals and awards, but above all, by businesses created, the decent jobs generated, and the opportunities often for our youth.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: With YouthConnekt Africa, let's build an Africa that no longer merely exploits its talents, and that develops at home a sports industry that is competitive, sovereign, and a source of shared prosperity. I look forward to very fruitful discussions here. Thank you for your kind attention.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. I love the energy in this room, I believe we're going to keep it going throughout our panel.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: As Paula mentioned, my name is Chara, I'm a strategist, I'm a youth mentor, but I'm also a proud member of the Metro Patriots Basketball Club. segments.text: But before we get into our questions, since our theme is legacy and practice, I want to ask each panelist to share with us the person or the opportunity that really opened the door for them in the sports industry. Let's start with you, Tata. You're all on top.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Chara.

I actually had my first opportunity through Tata, and the partnerships, the sports partnerships where they're giving the knowledge and the leadership of Clara Kamanzi at the time was a great opportunity that opened so many doors for me, and then of course I came out of a non-profit that will have the president of the BAL, and John O'Connor, who has been at the time, so it's been an incredible journey. segments.text: I would say it's a long story, but because we have no minutes in town to stay, strangely we need to make a spot, especially when I was to choose my career or what to learn. So basically I'm a physiotherapist, and from there I like sports, physiotherapy, and to explain to me the technical level. So this is actually a professor's talk.

segments.speaker: Christian (panelist)
segments.text: Hello, I'm Sande. I wasn't born into an academy, but I was born into a community which held the hopes in sports. So growing up, I had the people who saw what it meant, what sports meant, and that brought in the value in me, and they pushed me towards it.

segments.speaker: Christian (panelist)
segments.text: They told me, you can do it. So I just want to appreciate all the people who see their own talents and say, okay, you can do it, and also ask their parents to do it like in sports. Thank you so much.

segments.text: Good evening. I'm Matheus. I'm a Brazilian volleyball player.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: I'm so grateful to be here in Rwanda. My journey started when I was 10 years old, to practice volleyball. I met some people who pushed me, like Sande said, and encouraged us to have the increase of our talent in sports.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: And I'm here. That's it. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you for sharing your story. It reminds us that talent alone isn't enough. We need mentors, we need community, and we need encouragement.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: So I hope that you would do the same. I want to start with our first big question, and I want to hear from the athletes. Sandy first.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: From your time playing here in Rwanda, what does Rwanda already do very well in the area of sports? And then I would love for you to share one thing that you believe that Rwanda should invest in. Thank you again. I would just like to say that I came to Rwanda three years ago.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: This is my third year here, playing for the police. And when I came here, I wasn't the captain of the Kenya team. I would just say that when you come to Rwanda, the facilities themselves give you the morale to do it in volleyball.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: The professionalism that Rwanda has in sports is the one thing that pushes the players into it. If you don't have the motivation, then it's not there. Don't be motivated because you see everything is there.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: The professionalism in each and every club. Every club is being seen as a professional. If you have the lowest playing level, you'll be treated as a professional.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: And through that, you'll be motivated to do it even more. So I'll just echo what Rwanda is doing with the sports team. Because it's too good.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: And it's really promoting the African talent. And I can say that every country can echo what Rwanda is doing. Also, the infrastructure.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: You can see Amagoro Stadium, Petista. Every team has its own training court, which is better. Unlike some of the African countries.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: I'll just say that if every African country can echo what Rwanda is doing, we'll be at a different level. When I came here, I wasn't the captain of Kenya. But when I saw the things that were in front of me, I really put whatever energy I had.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: And it brought me to come out the best. And I was chosen as the captain of Kenya. So I'm so proud of Rwanda.

segments.speaker: Volleyball player from Kenya (Police)
segments.text: And I'm proud to be here. Thank you so much. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Mathias, tell us about your experience as an international athlete here.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: When I first came here to Rwanda, I was expecting something. But when I came here, I was surprised.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: Because the infrastructure, the Rwanda youth, the youth is amazing. It's amazing. Like, I'm taking care right now of our staff, so these things can motivate us to be on our high level every day, and that's a good thing, they're on the start this year, about the youth connection that's so far, I forgot the name, but it's a good connection closer than young people.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: Like, we are going to small cities to play there because it's a motivation to the young players to have closer players, professional players playing, and this is the motivation to them to come inside the sports to get basketball, volleyball, football, or whatever. Yeah, that's it, Rwanda is doing a great job. I'm so grateful to be here and it's an amazing experience of my life.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: Is there one area that you believe that Rwanda or other countries can learn to invest more in when it comes to sports from your experience as an athlete? I think it's on the high schools, in the second school, yes. I think that is most important tool to development of sports. Air development at that secondary school level.

segments.speaker: Matheus · Brazilian volleyball player
segments.text: Yes. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Okay, let's move from talent to ownership.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Teta, I'm coming back to you as our first contribution on this question. What needs to change for Africa to move from its position as a nurturer of wonderful talent in sports to becoming an owner of more of the value that sport creates? I mean, I think, and I kind of want to piggyback on what the athletes were saying. Africa has never been in a shortage of talent.

segments.speaker: Teta Ndejeru · BAL Country Director, NBA Africa
segments.text: I think that that has been clearly proven. In my experience through the basketball ecosystem is that we need to nurture the development of the ecosystem and development of the talent at the same time, right? Those two need to happen at the same time in order to really be able to create opportunity and legacy and for the youth to be able to see themselves not just as players but also maybe as marketers and content creators and the whole, to the point of the Minister, the Honorable Minister of Senegal, the ecosystem that it brings. And that is through development as well as building the ecosystem of sports through infrastructure, investment, and yeah, that's how you pass from a player to maybe a marketer to an investor and of course an owner.

segments.speaker: Teta Ndejeru · BAL Country Director, NBA Africa
segments.text: Very important pathway.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Teta. So the infrastructure is there within this context and in other contexts, but we need to nurture players at an earlier stage before investment and to happen simultaneously.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Teta. Sixth Bear, what are your thoughts on your perspective on the situation?

I think what Africa needs to invest in is an appropriate environment. When we talk about the environment, we need to think about the infrastructure, we need to think about capacity development because I believe the talent's goal abroad to look for, to look for a better environment where they'll be taken care of in different stages.

And I think we need really to invest in working on our environment, on proper infrastructures, but also being well-skilled, knowledgeable, to make sure they have natural talents, but also know how to create opportunities that will teach what talent is here and enjoy the value of our sports. Christian, would you like to add, especially on the value, increasing our value beyond our talent on the continent? Thank you, Marcel, from two perspectives. So one is the, what is a talent, what is a sport talent? I don't think we understand it on a bigger scale because we have been for so long considering sport athletes or sport talents only as athletes on the field.

But today if you check the whole sporting system, an athlete is at the centre of the market, but around the athletes there is a whole system. So if you want to move to proper ownership, I would say the first point is to widen our net and understand exactly what are the opportunities around the athletes. My colleagues are talking about broadcasts, social media, content, AI in sports, many, many other sectors around the sport.

So Africa has a huge opportunity to catch all these opportunities because we are not changing, we are adapting, so we are in the right stage. And if we manage to define all these opportunities and really focus on each intentionally, most of the athletes have defeated us before, that was an intentional approach. Putting an intentional approach, I believe now the whole system.

Secondly, we have to stop, as my colleague said, we have to stop thinking that the target for the sports market is outside Africa. We have been doing this for so many years, our athletes always have to go out in Africa to make a living. But yes, they have to go to the country, but now how can we make sure that we mitigate that by creating a good system in Africa? We have to invest in them and give them back so that they can feel valuable on the continent, they can make good money on the continent, and also invest in the continent.

So I think if we manage to fix those two points, make them a sports ecosystem, but also fight and intentionate for the sports market on the continent, to me I think the ownership will be for the world. Thank you. What you're all sharing is a very holistic approach to the sports ecosystem and the opportunities that we have in the sports economy.

So we know that, as you mentioned, there are many careers that can grow in the ecosystem, talent, ownership, investment to grow. Let's talk a bit more about capital. How can we encourage local sponsors and institutional investors to back led sports enterprises and also our domestic? How can we encourage more investment? It's not an easy one, but I'd like to preface something about it.

So first of all, to be interested based on international sports, we need first of all the existing opportunities we have. If we take an example, we have the government, which is really a very key component for bringing up people to invest in sports. We also have the talent, as they say, because I believe talents are everywhere.

The remaining task is to create the proper environment, which I believe the government is working on, like facilitating people who come to visit the companies and all the processes found out to sell sports and register their businesses. So I think in Rwanda, for instance, we need to attract people to invest in sports, but also we need to think of equipping people because people who come to invest, they're really human capital. So we also need to look into developing the skills and the management of people we have on site so that we get people to move with each other.
That's what I can say in terms of attracting sports as well. Investors trusting the system as well as the infrastructure and of course the political the highest levels. Thank you.

Teta, any thoughts on especially for youth-led enterprises or grassroots? I think two things. In Rwanda, there's an opportunity where government is investing in some of these in-building professional needs, like they're the foundational partner of the Basketball Africa League, and that has allowed for a lot of jobs to be created in that sector, in the basketball and sports sector. But I also think that when sports leagues are going to see sponsors or partners, they should also present themselves as a business, right? Like what is the return on investment? You should have the governance, you should have a business plan.

Why would somebody invest in you? How are you going to make that money back? And so I think there's an opportunity to professionalize how things are being managed right now and how they're presented to partners such as banks or some development partners as well. They're looking at how they can support the growth of the sport and to the leagues as professional teams that are building. What's the legacy plan? There should also be a pipeline.

So looking at those two things, there is definitely a responsibility of government to invest in that ecosystem as we're building the sector, and we see it in an amazing example here in Rwanda. It doesn't sound objective, but I think that also in the leagues there's an opportunity to professionalize the offering. I hope you're taking notes.

I think it's giving you a good game here on how to be investment ready so that sponsors come or say you engage with someone in this type of context, you would have something to present and professionalize. So that investor, there can be a match and alignment there. Thank you so much for that.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Because of our time, I would like to talk a little bit more on digital economy and technology when it comes to the growth of this economy. So we've talked about who owns, who plays the role in ownership, who's going to fund it. Let's look to the future and I think the future has already started that a lot of the careers in Africa's sport is going to be off the court, off the pitch.

It's going to be on screens, it's going to be online, it's going to be on apps and gaming centers. So I'd like to ask you Christiane and then also our athletes here, we'd love to get your perspective on this, about digital media and how gaming, esports, fan technology, the careers that come out of these opportunities and businesses for young Africans. And I would love to hear a bit more about opportunities for women in particular.

I will use the opportunity to talk about something in particular that they can give the opportunities on the digital economy of sports. So I also happen to be involved in motorsport. As many of you may know, we are hosting Formula One.
We are very blessed by the leadership of our country to bring Formula One back to the continent from the IAS 2013. There is an artery called Formula One. I will take a very concrete example.

In Formula One, we have 22 cars on each race. One car, the small car you see, has 300 plus sensors on the box. All those sensors transmit close to 1.1 million data points, information from those sensors.
And each of those sensors need young people like those one in this room to interpret the data from those sensors. Those are opportunities. If one car has 300 sensors, we do times 24 cars.

You can see that now. Now, the reason why I'm bringing this is to make sure that the young people in this room, when you talk about the digital part of sports, when you talk about the data part of sports, the data science behind it, let's really invest our time into meetings and understanding these opportunities so that by the time they come, we won't be asking, how can we be part of it? We should be ready to take part in those opportunities. You mentioned about the entry for women in sports.
Technology, science, media, it does not depend on gender. It does not depend on power. It does not depend on physical strength.
It depends on the brain. We are all equal. We are the same human being.

I would say the digital part of sports and the future of sports is allowing us to have an equal field and an equal entry point forever. It's not going to be about commitment. It's not going to be about how interested you are.
So I would encourage young ladies in the room. There are plenty of opportunities in motorsports. I would stay in motorsports and encourage them.
And everyone else, take time, start meeting now. The opportunities are coming, but the readiness is what's going to define how you'll be part of the future. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: That's a very important point. Suzanne, any thoughts on technology? Especially, I like how Christiane mentioned that it's almost a playing field, right? Everyone can engage. It makes it more inclusive.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Are there any new careers that you've found in your sector?
Thank you, Ms. Jasmine. He really touched every angle when it comes to technology and digital media. But I would say one thing.

Young people should stop now thinking of being more consumers. We need to also think of investing ourselves into the opportunities that are there. So we always say content creators, but I believe we don't say a lot in terms of creating content on spots.

So that one can be one opportunity, but also in terms of the data side of the thing, it can be an opportunity. So why don't we say just stop consuming, but also think of investing ourselves into existing opportunities. Thank you.
Thank you. Creating more time to...parting out more time to create and less consumption. And there's a lot of opportunity there, especially in the digital economy.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much. Any thoughts from you mentees on the digital economy? Do you engage at all with it? Or is there for anyone, or content creation or careers that are even beyond what you see yourself evolving as an athlete? Thank you so much. Of course, technology is everywhere.
I would just like to add the young, also young girls and the sports girls in our case. Let's use the opportunity in front of us. Let's not wait for the opportunity to locate us.
Because sometimes the question is, it is just in between us, but I hope to take the chance to create awareness about everything. And I would like also to add the community to support us. Follow us.
Push us towards doing whatever we want to achieve in life. Because of course if you support us, it's easy. It becomes very easy.
Technology is everywhere. Let's make use of it in a respectful way. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chara · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much. We have time for one more question. Earlier I asked you, who opened the door for you in the sports industry? And now I want to know, how are you paying it forward? How are you paying it forward with all of the knowledge and skills and opportunities that you have over your career? How are you helping someone else learn from you? I do my best in terms of motorsport where I sit as the president of the generation.

To make sure that we make it as inclusive as possible and also position our talent on the global stage. As I just mentioned, opportunities are there. Really to recap on what you said, capital is there, opportunities are there.

But commitment to me is what I keep pushing. All I can do is to try and market as much information as possible and create opportunities. I'm also involved in another initiative called Sport Biz Africa.
Where we invest in startups, sports startups. It's an annual event where local startups have great ideas in sports. We bring together investors, we even help those startups to be invested.

Because one of the elements you said, for example, the content. Now the athletes, they need to be considered not only as individuals but as products to be invested. So you need to have a brand, you need to have social media, you need to have your signature style so that someone can identify you as an interesting person.
So all I can say is I will keep doing as much as I can in terms of advocacy. And also to encourage young people. It's possible, you don't really have to wait for someone to come and pull your arm.
Go online, go outside, go learn. AI is there now. Let's not shy away from using AI.
It's important to use AI, adapt, open doors for yourself. Maybe you knock on 5 doors, they won't open. But maybe the 6th one will open.
So let's push as much as we can. Thank you. Thank you.

Antoine, how do you make it work? I think first, as players, we are doing a great job because whenever I pass, some people, even kids, stop me saying it. Because I have a group, they gave me a random name. It's SEKAMANA.

So everyone here knows me as SEKAMANA. So during the supermarket, gym, in the streets, when I come back to my home, the people will stop me and say, Hey SEKAMANA, I'm your fan, can I take a selfie with you? So I think I will pay for this one. I think we are doing a great job because we can connect close to the people about our job.
Because even sharing my international experience with the local people is very important. Thank you again. As he said, he is SEKAMANA, me, I'm Juanes.

The door was open for me, and also me, I cannot close the door. I'll keep the door open so that at least wherever I go, if I see a VIP who has that interest in sports and is willing to do it or she is willing to do it, at least whatever I have at hand, my peace of mind, encouragement, I'll use it to encourage her or him so that it will be easy for him going forward. And back in the village, maybe where we are coming from, we can go back and give back to the village because that's where we came from and that's where sports also is built.

So when we encourage people down there, that's where talent is built and when we encourage them, I think all of us may rise and that's the best thing to do. So myself, I'll just keep the door open by encouraging everyone to give their best. As the BAL, we have of course our social responsibility employer programs.

We also have a volunteer program in every market that we play in. We give the opportunity to about 100 youth to be able to come and experience our work and be exposed to production, sales, marketing, content, the 12 departments that make our organization. We also have dedicated employer programs.

As an entrepreneur, I'm part of the Growth to Scale program and so right now we're plugging in 10 entrepreneurs into the sporting ecosystem. It's important to create legacy, to create pipelines and I encourage everyone to please, if you have an idea, please reach out. Thank you.

I would say since the start of this job, all the responsibilities I have now, I've committed to the future. We have 16 countries in our region. I don't belong to any organization of FIFA so our hope is to administer FIFA more properly.

This is a program where we have 10 different projects and every project that I start working on, I make sure I get it. That's our commitment and that's one of my ways of giving back. But also I make sure I get my job done and share opportunities.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: It's an achievement now, and it belongs to all of us to do something different. In terms of creation, as I said earlier during the keynote, these games have allowed us to train young Africans. Young people will not only have fun, but we really wanted to select Africans as well.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: So, 6,000 volunteers have been trained. More than 450 young people have also been trained in events. So, these are skills that will actually remain.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: These skills are acquired, and we have made sure that these young people can be valued by a certification. That is to say, today, they can say, I was a manager in a certain field during the GeoGee. I have such skills.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: And they can also sell themselves in other competitions, in other events, whether it's sports or even cultural. I said earlier that Senegalese and African companies have won all the markets. These companies have also acquired skills.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: It was the first event in Africa, the first in Senegal, and the skills have been acquired. And, again, these skills are there. They remain there.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: And today, Rwanda has organized things, the orders have been organized, and we have already had exchanges with certain countries on how to transfer the skills acquired in Senegal to these countries. And it is really this African collaboration that will allow us, as I said, to make certain values real. So there is, and on the benefits, let's say, real, during these games, we have had totally full hotels in Senegal.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: So, these hotels have recruited, for several weeks, several young Senegalese. And it was the case in the restaurant. So, in reality, the benefits have been there.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: And the benefits are there as well, because these are events that we register in a strategic plan. So, then there are just infrastructures, of course, the material villages, these infrastructures that remain. The Olympic village that served to welcome the whole community of athletes was actually built on the university, on the university, in Montmartre, which had 7 buildings.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: So, all these 7 buildings were totally renovated, and in addition, we built 6 new buildings, with other infrastructures, of course, for the reservation. A beautiful village that will return to the students of Senegal. So, this is a benefit for young Senegalese.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: There is the Olympic pool, which is now not only an Olympic pool, but a complex, a complex on which we can do basketball, sports, and many other competitions. The same for the Ibarra stadium, which is now a complex, Ibarra 90 sports. So, all this remains for the youth to come.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: So, all this constitutes benefits. Thank you. Quickly, we must all learn from Senegal about the culture of sport.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: I grew up there, I had a culture of sport, and now we have arrived there, in Senegal, and it's been 20 years. But how to translate the culture of sport into a business of sport? That's the question. You talked about a very important way to take infrastructures that exist, to use existing infrastructures.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: As soon as you add new infrastructures, they remain to do something else. We will continue to generate money for these infrastructures. But how does the culture of sport, it means that every morning there is a sport that is done in Senegal, in the evening there is a sport that is done in Senegal.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: And how do we touch money? I want to come to Chad too, because I don't know much about Chad. You will have to explain yourself after that. That's an excellent question.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Indeed, every time we have foreigners who come, they are impressed by the number of Senegalese that we find on the curb in the morning or in the evening. And today we have invested a lot in this sport. It's not just to promote sport practice, it's also to develop the economy of sport.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Because the development of the economy of sport is also part of the national agenda of transformation, as well as of growth. Sport today allows us to create jobs, to create jobs, to create value, to really develop an economy. So how did it happen? First of all, it's these investments.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Because we live in a culture where we have money and we are able to attract investments and events. For example, Senegal was chosen to host the Games of Symphony in 2031. For me, this is also the result of investments, of events that are there to develop an economy.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: But beyond that, to develop the sport economy and transform all this into business, business for the government. And Senegal is part of all this. The Sport Code was adopted in 2010.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: This Sport Code replaces a charter that was adopted in 1994. Which means that we are really involved in this desire to transform the sporting ecosystem, to bring texts back to reality, to the reality of sport practice, and to facilitate investments in sport. One of the first things is already to develop sport as a mission of service to the people.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: To rethink the legal form of sports associations, sports clubs and clubs, so that it can be the society we live in today in which we can invest. There is the Fund for Sport Development, on which we also work. Objective Conventions that will allow us to work in good intelligence with the generations, to energize athletes.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Because that's also what transforming business is, to be able to develop athletes of good quality. We also have a program for the management of elites, which will allow us to bring Senegalese athletes to international competitions, to become performing athletes everywhere, but also and above all investors. Because high-level athletes are investors, and they can be investors.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: We see it with certain athletes, such as Saïd Oumaré and this one. But this possibility should not be underestimated with athletes. So the governance framework.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Then there is the support of community funds that evolve in the field of sport through financing, with advance funds, with grant funds. For example, in Senegal, there is a fund for theoretical investments that allows to support these small businesses and to reassure the investors by taking part in their investments. So all this will allow us to make the economy grow.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: I was talking about the course in Italy. In Italy, it is also the access of infrastructures to these small businesses that evolve in the field of sport. So that the access to infrastructures is rather linear.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: There is the training part. Training, training these small businesses in the management. We have agencies, institutions that are there for that.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: But I think there is also an important element, and this is really a message that I send to the population. Make a will today to develop the vision of sport, but not only the vision of governments. It is also the vision of the population.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: That is to say that the next generation will have a vision of sport. During the Olympic Games of Youth, I went out a lot to invite the Senegalese population to go out and see the competitions, to get involved. For example, so that we can go to other continents, take commercial investments to go see the Olympic Games, to go see the competitions, because it is also going to allow the ecosystem of sport and the ecosystem of business in the United States.

segments.speaker: Minister from Senegal (keynote)
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Moderator, ministerial panel
segments.text: Because I'm a teacher, I'm going to ask everyone to listen here and to keep the conversations light. I don't want to use my teacher voice, but I have a teacher voice.

segments.text: Okay. Mr. Minister, talk to me a little bit about Chad. What is your vision? What is happening? How is the business of sport going in Chad? No pressure, but in Senegal and in Rwanda, that's why I like you more in the middle, because otherwise it's hot.

segments.text: Thank you very much. First of all, I would like to applaud all these women who are in the sport. I'm going to try to be as small as possible.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: So first of all, let's talk about the economy of sport. I would like to ask you a small question to all the football fans in the room. We're going to have a little demonstration.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Who is the club that won the last European Champions League? Who can answer me? There are no football fans here? Mr. Minister, who won the last Champions League? It's too late. It was PSG. Now I'm going to ask you a second question.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Who won the last African Champions League? No one has the answer? This is extremely serious. This is the Mamaledi club without dance of South Africa who won the last African Champions League. To tell you already, by clarifying a little with these questions, many people know the clubs in Europe, the competitions in Europe, but very few people know sport and African football.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: And I think it's already the first economic opportunity that offers young people in Africa. To be people who sell their talents, African talents. The problem is that for me, the majority of young people that we have, even Africans, we are passionate people.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: We live from our passions. Unfortunately, in other economies, people find in their passions the sporting economy. This is the question that we, as members of the government, we must transform the calm passion in an economic opportunity.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Today, when we talk about a football match, volleyball, handball, there is a whole economy around a match. Whether it's football, whether it's the media, whether it's even the little lady who sells her little dolls in front of the stadium before the fans arrive to watch the match. And it's all these opportunities that we must transform into an opportunity of sustainable economy for young people.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Around a team of sport, a football team for example, there are several professions that exist. It's not just being a coach. We have the job of a journalist, we have the job of a nutritionist, we have the job of a physio.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Unfortunately, in Africa, we have very little expertise in these areas. And these are the areas that are lacking in our youth. And we must put in place this whole ecosystem so that our young people can access these professions.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Imagine, on the continent, there are very few young journalists. We have to call other foreign experts who are very dear to us, even though these are opportunities that are within our reach. So I call this little intervention to African youth not to vibrate at the level of our passions, but to transform our passions into an economic opportunity.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: So that's what we're trying to do at CHAT. We have a national institute of youth and sport to which we are putting specialized masters, short-term training for our leaders, so that they can be video analysts, construction workers, so that they can be on the market effectively and especially quickly. And I think, in any case, by developing all these expertise around sport, we can offer a lot of opportunities in the end, I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Moderator, ministerial panel
segments.text: Thank you. I've got the hard questions for the minister in Rwanda. So, the first question I have is, we are seeing a lot of infrastructure in sports, and I think the criticism for all in Senegal, in Rwanda, in all the big sports markets, is that we see a lot of huge infrastructure.

segments.speaker: Moderator, ministerial panel
segments.text: The stadium is beautiful, the Senegalese stadium is beautiful. What is happening for youth infrastructure, community infrastructure? How do you link the major infrastructure with the youth infrastructure and turn that into an economic engine? And I would say, young people want to know, how do I get into this sports business? I think the two major questions is how do we translate large infrastructure, as the minister from Senegal said, it attracts investment, so you need to create that infrastructure, it's not one or the other. Now that you created a big infrastructure, how does that turn into community infrastructure and bring back money into the country? Thank you very much, Anthony.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: First of all, since I'm part of the hosting teams, I want to welcome everybody. I want to thank my colleagues, ministers, for being here. Please join me in thanking all of them.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Particularly to the young people in the room. Are you there? Is that where you are? I can't see you. Are you there? So I must say, you are looking at this this morning and we are very excited to have you here and hope you enjoy it again.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: And the way you, as young people, we do it. You are? No? You did what? There we go. So, as we start and the question she just asked, I think we first of all need to put in context of what we are discussing this morning.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Why are we discussing sports? Because that is where it starts from. We are discussing sports because sports is life. Are we together? Sport is what? Sport is business.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Sport is what? And sport is entertainment. Sport is what? So it's life, it's business, it's entertainment. So I don't think there's anywhere you would find any opportunity as a young person for the future that will not be into one of those components.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We are investing as countries in sports because of the key roles it plays. When we say it's life, that means everything we are doing as government, Government of Rwanda, my colleagues and others, is first of all that sports is important even for well-being. It starts from there.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Because before we speak of the talent, before we speak of infrastructure, we've got to be healthy people. Isn't it? So sports is the first conductor or the first way of even keeping ourselves healthy. Because before you think, your brain needs to think straight.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: There's nothing that is going to help you even if you take coffee, even if you take I don't know, energy drink, name it, even if you see a therapist or anything. There's nothing that can help your mental health better than sports. If you agree with me, let us clap for that.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Applause So let's start from there. We are speaking of sports and we are speaking of sports in the three components. It's life, it is for us, it is for your well-being.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: If you are in this room and you have never exercised or you don't exercise regularly, that has to be a commitment from this YouthConnekt. The first connection you have to have is the connection with yourself. Are we together? And you can only do that through sports.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Your mental, your body, your mind, your emotions, everything. So sports is life. And any country or anyone that is looking at the future has to first of all look at life.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: And we like to say that youth is the future, which is true. In Africa, you all know this number. We all speak of 70% of our population being who? You.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: The people here and outside here. So it starts from there. The second component I mentioned is business.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: How do we transform that into business? And I'm going to answer to the question part of the questions you asked. As governments, it is our responsibility to work with private sector, to work with other players to create a platform. When we invest in stadiums, arenas, all the pitches, we are creating a community.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We are hoping for talent to develop. When you come and add a coffee shop, and you add selling the merchandises, and you add science and technology, and you add all those products you add there, you're creating value. So this is how the investment in the infrastructure becomes business.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: It's not just the building. It is everything else that happens in that building and outside the building. So the opportunity that comes there is you, young people with your innovation, with your creativity, with your ways of finding solutions to different problems you keep seeing in your communities, and you bring those solutions in those infrastructure, we are creating business.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: The third one is that sport is entertainment. Today, sport is, I don't know if I would say married or if it's a twin to creative industry. People in the creative industry in this room, do you agree with me? We can't do it without you.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Today, anything you're doing, yes, whether it's a football, basketball, any discipline, you marry it with singing, DJs, athletes, acrobats, everybody, painters, names, everything in the creative industry, and this is when you create the moment that will make people celebrate that sport themselves, the community, and also the creative vibe around it. So naturally, how do we change all these investments into community? The big picture is that government takes a lead into putting in place those infrastructure and the value behind those infrastructure comes from your entrepreneurship, comes from your ideas, comes from your innovation, and everything you create there that brings the jobs. Let me finish by giving an example.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: The government of Rwanda created Dike Arena, invested in Dike Arena. Today, at one event we're having at Dike Arena, we create almost 2,500 jobs around that. That is in every service you're having there.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Yes, please. That's very important. So many areas that are bringing young people into that.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: So the vision is that the state will put in place but the next step is now how do we go in the communities? We're having a plan as government of Rwanda now to work with community and also private sectors to have what we call community playgrounds because it's important to have also playgrounds, beaches, and all that in the community but remember, the most important is not the beach, the court, the most important is the business around it and that is where you apply. Thank you. So before we open up to questions because we want young people to address directly, I want to do a quick fire round where think about yourself as a government investor.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: What are the businesses or what are the areas that the government is interested in? That means if a young person comes and you as an investor for the government, what are the areas that are you interested in? So we'll start with the chat, no pressure. A young person, what is the business that would catch your attention? Which one would you like to deal with today? You can continue talking. I'm more in the development of the economy.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: If we look at all the selected channels that highlight the competitions, it is mostly European channels. And we, the African nationals, will highlight our own talents. Not only the sporting talents, but also the media.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Today, what I want to see when I turn on the TV is African journalists who are internationally well-known and who talk about our championships, our clubs, our best players, our best channels. And I think there are a lot of platforms that highlight what we do in Africa. There are very beautiful things that we do in Africa.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: And for me, if I had money to invest, it would be the implementation. Maybe the government, you have a lot of money to invest. No, I don't think so.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: So you don't see it as necessary? No, I don't see it as necessary. Because when we highlight a talent, the fact that it is an integration, we highlight a country, we highlight a culture, a tradition that maybe this player that we highlight, maybe he will be taken in the best clubs in the world. And behind him, there is a whole community that will live.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: So if we highlight our champions of Tonin, the whole economic chain will follow. In any case, for me, this is the main objective. Mediatization, for the moment, there is a lot of, I would say, there is a lot of business in this.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: And I think it should be highlighted because it exists, I think, at the level of Senegal. So, if I were an investor, I think that Africa will organize more and more events. I think things will change, things are changing anyway.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: And for a very long time, when we had some competitions like AFRON, every time I saw in the streets everything that is goodies or small equipment, that is to say jerseys, flags, flags, all the little things that are marketed during sporting events, I always asked myself the question, why didn't we do it in Africa? In fact, when we organize these events, we free industries from other countries. And as I said earlier, sporting activity, or at least African events, will develop. It will be the tendency.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: If I were an investor, it would be in this sector, in this segment of equipment, goodies, of course, after what my colleague Buchat said. And also, this market, for it to develop, we need what we said during the ceremony, what President Kagame said, this collaboration between ministers, this opening of the free-trade zone, for it to become a reality, so that young Africans, not only the Senegalese market, but also the African market, will be able to sustain themselves. Okay, minister, we've heard digital media, we've heard merchandising, which is very important, if you are an investor, what will you invest in? Well, I will invest in the tools, in what Chai said, and the last point I will add is any technology that is going to make it easier, talent development, that is going to make it easier, facility management, because we are investing in those facilities, that is going to make it easier the way sport is practiced in this business.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: So any thinking, innovative thinking, using science and technology, that is going to make sports faster, more accessible, and more productive. Great. So, we are going to have some questions.

segments.speaker: Audience member · Liberia

segments.text: If we have time, we will come back. We will come back.
Mr. Minister of Chad, we will start with you. But it's a question for all the ministers in Africa, all our athletes, if you give them a contract. Sometimes, I have professionals who play for me.

Now, how do we change that?

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Thank you very much for the question of my compatriot. I think we have to create all the conditions. When we have athletes who leave abroad, it's because all the conditions are united abroad.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: So we have to put all the conditions. The first condition are the infrastructures. We have very good infrastructures and infrastructures that allow us to compete well.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Unfortunately, sometimes, I'll give you an example. When we have a footballer who plays internationally, he plays on the tennis. But most of the time, in Africa, we play on synthetic.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Why do we play on synthetic? Because it's easier to intervene. And if we want to attract our own athletes, we have to be well-trained in the infrastructures and well-trained in our governance. Because often, we have governance problems within the sports federations.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: We have the president of the federation who stays 15 or 20 years. The president of the federation unfortunately, they have never done the necessary to put the conditions for their teams. And also, the remuneration and especially the status of the athlete.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Today, in the majority of African countries, the athletes don't move from their sport, unfortunately. They are forced to do other jobs to meet their needs. So, we have to go more towards the professionalization of our championships, of our sports, so that our athletes can have contracts and live fully of their sport.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: It's a huge challenge. It's true that elsewhere, they are ahead because they don't see sport as an entertainment. They see it as a development tool.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Thank God, in Africa, there is a new generation of young ministers. And I think that the heads of governments and heads of states understand that investing in sport and investing in youth is the future. We saw a few weeks ago the Olympic Games of youth in Dakar.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: In a few years, I think in 2030, we will see the World Cup in Morocco as well. Morocco, Portugal, Spain. I can tell you that things are changing.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Governments are investing in sport. So, it's up to us to put the conditions so that our athletes, especially the young ones, can play in Africa. It's a problem everywhere.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: How do you do it? It's a problem everywhere. That's what the minister said and that's what we've come to. In reality, it's a work in progress.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Things won't be done in one day. Someone said, and I think it's important for the youth to have this message, it's not accepting when people say that things don't change in Africa. In reality, as I said earlier, changes are there.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: I come from the private sector and in the private sector, we often said that we need to celebrate those small steps, those small wins. And we do it in a very, very conscious way. All these infrastructures that we are developing develop a sporting ecosystem.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: I spoke earlier about the sport code. The sport code is there to professionalize sports and to institutionalize everything that is deontology in sport. Because it's often said that deontology in sport affects federations, athletes and the ecosystem around it.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: In Senegal, we launched a program to identify youth, to identify sectors, sports disciplines, and to concretely support these athletes through scholarships, through taking charge of certain things, especially what is expensive for an athlete, including training for the national stadium, and all these things, and to prepare these athletes to go to competitions and to win in Senegal. Today, we have an athlete, a gentleman, who is shining in athletics, and I would really like to applaud this young lady who made the news today. And we are proud that she accepted to come here with the colours of Senegal, because there is an institutional support here, but also because the private sector is also involved.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: Today, the private sector must be accompanied by Orange, which is sponsoring. These are examples that will gradually allow our African talents to accept to stay in Africa. I would like to come back to the question of how to go from micro-businesses around the stadium to real businesses.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: I would say that the private sector in general asks what is my incentive to invest in sports? How to go from a small business in 30 seconds to a big business around the stadium in the course of scientific negotiations? She asked, I have a micro-business, I sell babies next to the stadium, how can I become a big business, a merchandising business? It's your idea, you have to have a plan. I speak as a former actor of the private sector. You have an idea, you have to have a strategic plan.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: You may ask today, what is your ambition in 10, 15 years? You want to be a big business in this sector, that's it. It's also to get informed. Earlier, during the previous panel, someone said that youth must accept to look for information, to think out of the box.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: First, it's yourself. Then, there are all the support mechanisms. It's true that in Africa, we have this difficulty of accessibility to information.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: That's a reality. Now, young people have to take this step, to look for information, to see what the support mechanisms are. For example, in Senegal, for small businesses, there are mechanisms.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: For example, we support professional training and technical support. Sometimes, you start a business without having the technical skills to bring it to the next level. You have to go to these institutions to support them.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: I was talking about the Guarantee Fund for Priority Investments, which grants these young people who struggle to find funding in classical institutions. All these instruments allow you to go to information, to infrastructures, to have a strategic plan, and maybe, to conclude on this point, on the business, in the field, we always say that to grow a business, you need people, tools, and processes. You have the people, you work on the human part.

segments.speaker: Minister from Chad
segments.text: If you have a team, you make sure that you have the competencies to grow, and you make sure that you have the tools, and also, you put in place the processes. Sometimes, we lack those processes in our businesses. Thank you.

segments.text: Final two questions. Maybe you can talk to us, Minister Ronda. You can talk to us about the SOMA program.

segments.text: And also, answering the question from Uganda, which is, what can other countries learn from you? How do we make local championships as popular as the ball? Ball brings NBA money. segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: First of all, we learn from each other. As Ronda, thanks to our visionary leader, there are steps we've been able to achieve in these two years, but we are also learning. So, let us not think that we've got somewhere that we have to share.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We are also learning. We are learning from Senegal, China, and other countries. But I want to emphasize this answer to my sister was this question.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: First of all, when you are attracting these international events, and I would like all the young Africans in this room to follow. Give me just one minute. It is a matter of dignity as Africans to start with.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Yes, you can clap for her. Because we are in a time, and this is very important as young people in Africa to understand that and to be having that end in mind in everything we are doing. Everything we need to venture into, we need to have that purpose.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Why are we doing this? For Ronda, it's a matter of dignity as Africans, as veterans of course. We have a history, we have the past we've gone through which has taught us that if you want something, you have to go for it and nobody should tell you that you cannot do it. Yes? So, when we go for those partnerships, Arsenal, Atlético, PSG and others, it has always started from that thinking that Michael was saying.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We are capable. We can do for that. We have to prepare.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We have to go for that purpose. It will not come as a second letter, but it's a matter of dignity as an African. Second, it's a matter also of knowing what you're committing to.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: The African is an African. We are going to have a next one in Ronda that is for the entire African community. And that is why I want to invite all of you, young people, as Christian mentioned it, this is the moment.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Start bringing your ideas. But let me challenge you. You need to bring innovative ideas.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: You are not all going to be sellers of merchandises. You are not all going to be the sellers of the same product. This is the moment where the most competitive is going to be the one who is investing in family love with something that is unique and that is game changing.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: I know this is a language sometimes we don't want to hear as young people. We all want to bring the same business and we all want to be financed. Competition is tight.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: You've got to take time to invest in your own creativity so that you bring on table something that is going to be a game changer. Otherwise, I'm sorry, not everybody is going to do the same thing and be able to get the same access to funds and the ways you've been committed. So, how other countries do that, we believe that if we're intentional as Africans in terms of saying this is our time to do it as Africans, to do it in Africa and that it benefits Africans, everybody can do it.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We did the championship of cycling, the world championship, they did the youth Olympic Games, there's more coming, but the key word is what is your ending mind? The ending mind is about Africa, doing it as an African for your pride, for your dignity but you do it as an African because your skills and opportunities will benefit your own countries to start with and then after it will also benefit others. So that's the only thing I can say in that. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: How do we make sure that our local championships are also committed? First of all, we have to clean our championships. When I say clean, it means first of all as athletes, we have to be athletes who are focused, who are disciplined, who are disciplined, who are committed. Nobody is going to come and invest in the loser.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Hello? No one. Nobody is going to bring... So as athletes, that's where we start from. Governance of our championships, they have to be professionalized.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Our federations, our clubs, the competition, the level of competition has to be professionalized and clean. Third, we have to show the business opportunity that is there. I hope my brother from Liberia says this.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: That is where you're going to be competitive. And we have to create products that make our championships celebrate. Young people, we need to have a YouTube Africa.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Hello? We need to have a Netflix Africa. You understand what I mean? We need to get to a point where we own our products, we sell our products, we get money. Today, sports generate money.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Of course, more than all sports. Do your research. Every money, every tiny investment that comes in sports now is more about what you're selling, how you're selling it, to whom you're selling it.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: So we have to be honest with ourselves. Our local championships will be able to attract investment to the global if we are having talents that are being competitive, that are being professional, if the governance of our championships are professional, and if we are selling, this is where people are going to be able to invest in our championships. Last but not least, she asked about the SONDA program.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: That's one of the programs we are doing and learning from others also about grassroots development. This is a program that is in secondary schools. We started with a few disciplines.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We'll continue with more disciplines. And the target is to develop the talent under 13, under 15, and under 17, because that is the only way we'll be able to be competitive in the future. So we identify the talent, we nurture them, we invest in infrastructure in those schools, and we partner, work with the different clubs and the leagues, to make sure that every holiday those kids that are going to that program, they have a week where they're doing camps, they're all together, they're training, they're competing, they're learning.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: We are talking about discipline, we are talking about being talents that have a code of ethics and so forth, and then in big holidays they spend two weeks, and this is something we are trying to build, focusing on grassroots development and talent development. Because the future or the biggest resource that Africa has is our talent in everything we do. So we need to sharpen it, and we need to be a factory of our talent that is going to serve our markets, be competitive in Africa, but even globally, as we develop it from home.

segments.speaker: Hon. Nelly Mukazayire · Minister of Sports, Rwanda
segments.text: Thank you. Okay. So we heard from the ministers, there are opportunities in digital media, talent scouting, merchandising, technology that facilitates everything from facility management to sports of athletes.
